title: Three times a day (Berakhot 26b)
hookLine: morning, afternoon and evening prayer are linked to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, or to the Temple offerings

cards: Breakfast, lunch, dinner. Waking up, the afternoon slump, winding down at night. Most people already live by a rhythm of three, and three times a day the mood tips into something new.

Jewish prayer hangs on the same three hinges: shacharit in the morning, minchah in the afternoon, ma'ariv in the evening. The Talmud asks where these three times came from. It gives two answers, and keeps both.

teach.b: In Berakhot, on page twenty-six, Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Hanina says the patriarchs set the prayers. Abraham set the morning: the Torah says he rose early and went to the place where he had stood before God.

teach.h: ISAAC: IN THE FIELD AT EVENTIDE.
teach.b: Isaac set the afternoon: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide."

teach.h: JACOB: MEETING THE PLACE AT NIGHT.
teach.b: Jacob set the evening: night was falling when he came upon a certain place, and the Talmud reads that word, vayifga, as meeting God in prayer.

Rabbi Yehoshua son of Levi says something else: the prayers match the Temple's daily offerings, morning and afternoon, with the evening prayer matching the parts that burned on the altar through the night.
The Talmud doesn't throw either answer away. It weaves them together: the patriarchs began these prayers, and the rabbis tied them to the offerings.
One picture says prayer is personal, a man walking alone in a field at dusk. The other says it's shared and regular, like the Temple's daily service.
Both stay on the same page.

And so a week that began in the Torah's last chapters, with Moses seeing the land from the mountain and buried where no one knows, ends inside the prayer book: its order, and now its three times a day.

how: Observant Jews pray three services daily: shacharit in the morning, minchah in the afternoon and ma'ariv (also called arvit) in the evening, often with a minyan, a quorum of ten, in synagogue.

o: he slept: Jacob's rest under the open sky
he wrestled: Jacob's long night with the angel
he met: Jacob's encounter, read as prayer

games.q: three hinges of the day — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud gives only one origin for the three prayers
the patriarchs, or the Temple offerings, and it keeps both.
Isaac went out to meditate in the field at eventide
Genesis 24:63, read as the afternoon prayer.

games.q: two rabbis disagree: the three prayers come from the patriarchs, or from the Temple's daily offerings. what does the Talmud do?
games.why: Berakhot 26b: the patriarchs established them, and the rabbis linked them to the offerings. personal and shared at once.

practice: Pick three moments, one for morning, one for afternoon, one for night, and tie each to something you already do: the first coffee, a late-afternoon break, brushing your teeth.
Picture stopping at each for three breaths, like hinges in your day. If you pray, it could be a prayer you know; if not, the pause alone is enough.

wordCard.voice: Vayifga. He met, or encountered — the word the Talmud reads in Jacob's story as meeting God in prayer, one root of the three daily prayer times.

orig.note: Hebrew: the morning, afternoon and evening prayers.
